title: Quantifying How Much GCG Suffix Transferability Degrades Across Model Size

original_idea.problem: Whether larger models within the same family are more or less resistant to GCG suffixes optimized on smaller models is not characterized.
original_idea.direction: Optimize GCG suffixes on Llama-3-8B, evaluate transfer to Llama-3-70B and 405B. Measure per-prompt ASR across sizes.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If suffixes transfer small-to-large, an attacker with a consumer GPU can jailbreak frontier models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: transfer scaling relationship -> affects threat model assumptions. Important characterization but the gap between the scaling finding and a safety improvement is underspecified.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: GCG optimization requires significant GPU resources and familiarity with adversarial optimization code. Running 70B/405B models requires substantial compute. Advanced for beginners with medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Deliverable requires sustained effort: running GCG optimization (computationally expensive), then evaluating transfer across 3 model sizes. Multiple resource-intensive steps.

novelty.reasoning: Zou et al. (2023) demonstrated GCG transferability across models including from smaller to larger ones, and noted smaller models are more vulnerable. 'The Resurgence of GCG Adversarial Attacks on Large Language Models' (arXiv:2509.00391, 2025) confirmed GCG attacks succeed against a 20B model. However, a systematic within-family scaling study (e.g., Llama-3-8B -> 70B -> 405B) measuring per-prompt ASR degradation as a function of size has not been published as a controlled experiment. The qualitative direction is known but the quantitative scaling curve within a single model family remains a gap.
